**4. [E] Which of these get a range table with $O(1)$ queries: $\min$, $\oplus$, $\gcd$, a product when one element may be $0$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only $\oplus$. The table needs an inverse to cancel the unwanted prefix: XOR cancels itself ($x\oplus x = 0$). $\min$ and $\gcd$ are idempotent — combining $a$ with itself changes nothing, so nothing cancels — and a product has a division inverse only where no zero is present (@sec-pref-other).
:::

**5. [E] One range-add update costs how many writes to the difference array, whatever the range length?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Two: $+v$ at the first cell and $-v$ just past the last. An update covering the entire array writes $+v$ to `d[0]` and $-v$ to `d[n]` and nothing else (@sec-pref-diff).
:::

**6. [E] Given the difference array $d$ of $a$, recover $a$. Given $a$, recover $d$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a$ is the prefix of $d$ (`run += d[i]`), and $d[i] = a[i] - a[i-1]$ with $a[-1]=0$. The two operations are exact inverses, which is why "prefix of a difference" and "difference of a prefix" both return the original (@sec-pref-diff).
:::

**7. [E] Count the subarrays of $[1,-1,1,-1]$ whose sum is $0$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Prefix sums: $0,1,0,1,0$. Value $0$ occurs three times ($\binom{3}{2}=3$ pairs) and value $1$ twice ($\binom{2}{2}=1$): **4** subarrays — $[0,2), [2,4), [1,3), [0,4)$. Equal prefixes, not zero-sum prefixes, are the counting rule (@eq-pref-hash).
:::

**8. [E] For "count subarrays with sum $=k$", what cheaper technique exists if all elements are positive?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A sliding window: with positives the window sum grows as you extend and shrinks as you release, so one $O(n)$ pass with $O(1)$ space suffices. The map version costs $O(n)$ space but survives negatives (@sec-arr-scan, @sec-pref-p2-a).
:::

**9. [M] Write the 2D query for a judge that gives 1-based inclusive corners $(x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$P[x_2][y_2]-P[x_1-1][y_2]-P[x_2][y_1-1]+P[x_1-1][y_1-1]$. The table's padding row and column make $x_1=1$ or $y_1=1$ read zeros instead of needing a branch (@sec-pref-2d, @sec-pref-p4-a).
:::

**10. [M] How many writes does a rectangle-add need in a 2D difference array, and how do you rebuild?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Four: $+v$ at $(r_1,c_1)$, $-v$ at $(r_1,c_2)$, $-v$ at $(r_2,c_1)$, $+v$ at $(r_2,c_2)$ for the half-open rectangle $[r_1,r_2)\times[c_1,c_2)$. Rebuild with one 2D prefix pass. The signs are the *mirror image* of the query formula — the update is the inverse operation of the read (@sec-pref-2d).
:::

**11. [M] If $m_v$ prefix sums fall in remainder bucket $v \bmod k$, give a closed formula for the number of divisible subarrays, and check it on $[4,5,0,-2,-3,1]$, $k=5$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every pair of equal remainders is one answer, so $\sum_v \binom{m_v}{2}$. Prefix sums are $0,4,9,9,7,4,5$ with remainders $0,4,4,4,2,4,0$: $m_0=2$, $m_4=4$, $m_2=1$, giving $1+6+0=\mathbf{7}$ — LeetCode's expected answer. The incremental `ans += cnt[r]` computes the same sum without a second pass (@sec-pref-p2-b).
:::

**12. [M] Build the prefix XOR of $[1,3,4,8]$ and answer the query $[1,2]$ (inclusive) with two reads.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$P = [0,1,2,6,14]$. The answer is $P[1]\oplus P[3] = 1\oplus6 = 7$, and indeed $3\oplus4=7$. The shared prefix $P[1]$ appears twice and cancels (@sec-pref-p5-b).
:::

**13. [M] An element is a *leader* if it is greater than or equal to everything to its right. Find the leaders of $[16,17,4,3,5,2]$ and state the invariant of your one-pass algorithm.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Scanning right to left, keep `best` $=\max$ of everything already seen: $2$ is a leader, then $5$ ($>2$), then $17$ ($>5$); $4$ and $3$ lose to $5$, and $16$ loses to $17$. Leaders, in original order: $[17,5,2]$ at indices $1,4,5$. This is a suffix table for $\max$ — no inverse is needed because you only ever read the whole suffix (@sec-pref-other).
:::

**14. [M] `out[i]` = product of all elements except `a[i]`, in $O(1)$ extra space and without division. Give the two passes and their invariants.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Forward: `out[i] = out[i-1]*a[i-1]`, leaving `out[i]` $=\prod_{k<i}a[k]$. Backward: keep `run` $=\prod_{k>i}a[k]$ in one variable and multiply `out[i] *= run`. Both invariants hold by construction, and no cell is ever read after it is finalised (@sec-pref-p5-a).
:::

**15. [M] For which of these can you binary search the first valid cut instead of scanning all of them: (a) all $a_i \ge 0$, (b) $a_i$ may be negative? Give a concrete counterexample for the other case.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only (a): non-negative cells make $P[k]$ non-decreasing in $k$, so "left $\ge$ right" becomes a suffix of true answers. (b) fails — for $[10,4,-8,7]$ the three cuts give left sums $10,14,6$ against right sums $3,-1,7$, so the predicate is true, true, **false**: not monotone, and a binary search can miss the answer $2$ (@fig-pref-p6, @sec-pref-p6-a).
:::

**16. [H] Updates and queries now **interleave**: add $v$ to $[l,r]$, then ask for a point or a range value, $2\cdot10^5$ of each. Why does the difference array fail, and what replaces it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The difference array amortises its cost by rebuilding *once*, at the end; rebuilding after every update is $O(n)$ per operation, and reading a point from `d` without rebuilding is meaningless because a cell's value is a prefix of `d`, not the value itself. You need a structure that keeps prefixes available under point updates — a Fenwick (binary indexed) tree or a segment tree with lazy propagation, both later volumes (@sec-pref-p3).
:::

**17. [H] Count subarrays whose sum is **at least** $K$, with negatives allowed. The map trick handles equality; what does the inequality cost?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
You need pairs $(i,j)$ with $P[j]-P[i]\ge K$, i.e. for each $j$, the number of earlier prefixes $\le P[j]-K$ — a *rank* query over values seen so far, not a key lookup. That is $O(n\log n)$ with a sorted structure or a Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values (the classic "count of range sum" problem); a merge-sort counting pass does the same without a tree. The hash map cannot answer "$\le$" because it has no order (@sec-pref-hash).
:::

**18. [H] For the divisible-by-$k$ count, when is the bucket array the wrong choice?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
When $k$ is large relative to $n$ or is not an input bound at all: $O(k)$ memory and $O(k)$ initialisation lose to the $O(\min(n,k))$ distinct prefix remainders in a hash map. Also, with $t$ test cases and a fresh $k$ each time, re-zeroing a $k$-sized array costs $t\cdot k$ — use a map, or timestamp the buckets (@sec-pref-p2-b, @sec-arr-p5).
:::

**19. [H] "Flip every bit in a $k$-long window, minimum number of flips to make all bits $1$" (LC 995-style). Why is this a difference-array problem, and what changes in the template?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Scan left to right; the first $0$ *forces* a flip starting there, so the greedy choice is unique. You must know how many of the active flips cover the current cell — exactly a coverage count — so keep a difference array over flip **parity**: `d[start] += 1`, `d[start+k] -= 1`, and read the running sum modulo $2$. The only change from @sec-pref-diff is that the accumulator is XOR/parity rather than a sum, because a flip is its own inverse (@sec-pref-other).
:::

**20. [E] Prefix sums are stored modulo $M = 10^9+7$, and $P[2] = 5$, $P[6] = 3$. What is the sum of $a[2:6)$ modulo $M$, and what goes wrong in C++ if you write `p[6] - p[2]`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(3 - 5 + M) \bmod M = 10^9+5$. In C++ `p[6] - p[2]` is $-2$: the true sum is congruent to $-2$, but a negative value is not a valid remainder and breaks later comparisons or array indexing. Add $M$ before taking `%` (@eq-pref-mod). Python's `%` returns $10^9+5$ directly.
:::

**21. [E] An array of words and many queries "how many words in positions $[\ell, r)$ start with a vowel?". What table do you build?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The prefix sums of the indicator array $b[i] = 1$ if word $i$ starts with a vowel, else $0$. Then each query is $P[r]-P[\ell]$: a count is a sum of zeros and ones (@sec-pref-def).
:::

**22. [M] Find the length of the longest subarray of $[1,-1,5,-2,3]$ with sum $3$, and say which map you used.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Prefixes: $P = 0,1,0,5,3,6$. First occurrences: $0\to0$, $1\to1$, $5\to3$, $3\to4$, $6\to5$. At $j=4$ ($P=3$) the target $P-3=0$ first appeared at index $0$: length $4$, the range $[1,-1,5,-2]$. At $j=5$ ($P=6$) the target $3$ first appeared at $4$: length $1$. Answer $4$, from a **first-index** map that is never overwritten (@sec-pref-hash).
:::

**23. [M] Intervals $[s,e)$ with $s, e$ up to $10^9$; find the largest number that overlap at one point. Why not a difference array, and what replaces it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A difference array would need $10^9$ cells. Coverage changes only at interval ends, so store $+1$ at each $s$ and $-1$ at each $e$ in a map, sort the $2u$ keys and sweep, keeping the running coverage and its maximum: $O(u\log u)$ time, $O(u)$ space, independent of the coordinate range (@sec-pref-diff).
:::

**24. [H] Count the ways to cut an array into three non-empty parts with equal sums, $n \le 5\cdot10^5$, values may be negative. Why is the two-pointer method of @sec-pref-p6-b not the right tool, and what is?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With negatives the prefix sums are not monotone, so a pointer cannot move in one direction only. And the question is a count, not a maximum. Check $3 \mid P[n]$; then scan the second cut $j$ from $2$ to $n-1$, adding $1$ to a counter whenever $P[j-1] = P[n]/3$ (a first cut becomes available) and adding the counter to the answer whenever $P[j] = 2P[n]/3$. $O(n)$, and the all-zero array gives $\binom{n-1}{2}$ with no special case (@sec-pref-split).
:::

## Interview questions

**1. What is a prefix-sum table, and why is $P[0]=0$ the convention that removes your off-by-one bugs?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$P[i]=\sum_{k<i}a[k]$ for $i\in[0,n]$: $n+1$ cells, each the sum of everything *strictly below* its index. Then any half-open range is $P[r]-P[\ell]$, and an empty range reads $0$ for free. The alternative — $P[i]=\sum_{k\le i}a[k]$ — forces `if (l == 0)` in every query (@sec-pref-def, @sec-arr-ranges).
:::

**2. Why is the difference array called the inverse of the prefix sum?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`prefix(d)` recovers $a$ and `difference(a)` recovers $d$, so the two passes undo each other. Operationally, a difference array is "a range update written as two point updates": $+v$ where the range starts, $-v$ where it ends. That is why one rebuild pass converts $u$ range adds from $O(nu)$ to $O(n+u)$ (@sec-pref-diff).
:::

**3. $n,q \le 2\cdot10^5$, the array is immutable, each query is a range sum. Derive the complexity you are allowed to write.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$O(nq) = 4\cdot10^{10}$ is hopeless against a $\sim10^8$ budget, so the answer must be $O(n+q)$: build the table in $O(n)$, answer each query in $O(1)$. The constraint pair ($n$ large *and* $q$ large) is the recognition signal; if $q$ were $1$, no table is needed (@sec-pref-p1, @sec-arr-cost, @sec-cx-budget).
:::

**4. Count subarrays with sum $k$. Why not a sliding window, and what is the invariant of the map solution?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Negatives break the window: extending can lower the sum, so "shrink while too big" has no justification. The map solution walks the prefix sums and uses $\sum a[i:j) = k \iff P[i] = P[j]-k$; the invariant is that before index $j$, `seen[v]` counts the prefix indices with value $v$, so `seen[p-k]` is exactly the number of legal left ends — one lookup per element, $O(n)$ (@sec-pref-hash, @sec-pref-p2-a).
:::

**5. Why does "divisible by $k$" shrink a hash map to an array of size $k$, and what is the trap in C++?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$k \mid (P[j]-P[i])$ iff $P[j]\equiv P[i]\pmod k$, so the key is the remainder and there are only $k$ of them — time $O(n+k)$, space $O(k)$. The trap: C++'s `%` returns a negative remainder for a negative left operand, so `cnt[r]` indexes out of bounds; normalise with `((r % k) + k) % k`. Python's `%` never returns a negative (@sec-pref-p2-b).
:::

**6. Which operations get a prefix table, and what do you do when the operation has no inverse?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Anything associative with an inverse — a group: $+$, $\oplus$, and $\times$ away from zeros. Without an inverse ($\min$, $\max$, $\gcd$, product-with-zeros) you cannot cancel a prefix, so you build a **suffix** table instead and combine a prefix with a suffix, which answers "everything to my left/right" but not "the range in the middle" (@sec-pref-other, @sec-pref-p5-a).
:::

**7. Derive the 2D rectangle formula. Why is the corner added rather than subtracted?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$P[r_2][c_2]$ is the anchored block; removing $P[r_1][c_2]$ deletes the top strip and removing $P[r_2][c_1]$ deletes the left strip — and the top-left rectangle $P[r_1][c_1]$ lies in both strips, so it was deleted twice and must be added back once. Inclusion–exclusion: alternate signs by how many sets you removed (@sec-pref-2d, @sec-pref-p4-a).
:::

**8. Product of array except self: the interviewer says "no division". Why, and what does it cost you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Division by zero: one zero makes the total product zero, so `total/a[i]` is either undefined or wrong for every cell. The two-pass version — forward left products into the output, backward with one running right product — is $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ auxiliary, and has no case analysis at all (@sec-pref-p5-a).
:::

**9. Find Pivot Index: why do you test *before* accumulating the current element?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The pivot is excluded from both sides. Testing first means `left` is the sum of $a[0{:}i]$ only, and the right side is `total - left - a[i]`; it also returns the *leftmost* pivot, since you return at the first match. Accumulating first would silently include $a[i]$ on the left (@sec-pref-p1-b).
:::

**10. When may you binary search or two-pointer over cut positions, and when must you scan them all?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only when the prefix sum is monotone in the cut position, which needs every element non-negative. All-positive problems (CF 1006C, "split into three equal sums") allow $O(n)$ two pointers or $O(n\log n)$ searches. Once negatives are allowed (LC 2270, LC 560) the prefix rises and falls, the predicate is not monotone, and a scan of all $n-1$ cuts is the honest bound (@sec-pref-p6-a, @sec-pref-p6-b).
:::

**11. Where exactly does 64-bit arithmetic become mandatory in this chapter's problems?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In the *table*, not just the answer: $2\cdot10^5$ values up to $10^9$ sum to $2\cdot10^{14}$. Greg and Array multiplies a run count of $10^5$ by a delta of $10^5$ and then sums $10^5$ such terms — $10^{15}$. And in C++ widen before the operation: `(long long)a * b` is fine, `a * b` assigned to a `long long` has already overflowed (@sec-arr-cost, @sec-pref-p3-b).
:::

**12. Your table is $O(n)$ space, but the interviewer asks for $O(1)$. What can you always give up?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The table, if you only need one prefix at a time. A single left-to-right scan can carry `left` as a scalar plus the total, which turns pivot/split/count-equal-suffix problems into $O(1)$ space (@sec-pref-p1-b). What you cannot give up: queries that revisit arbitrary ranges, or a hash map that must remember every prefix value — those genuinely need their $O(n)$.
:::

**13. Two accepted-looking solutions to "count subarrays divisible by $k$" have the same $O(n)$ idea, but one times out on a judge with many test cases. What are the usual culprits?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Constant factors and hidden per-test costs, not the idea. An ordered `map` costs $O(\log n)$ per operation where a bucket array of size $k$ (or an `unordered_map`) costs $O(1)$. Allocating or clearing a $k$-sized array for every test case costs $t \cdot k$ in total even when the inputs are tiny — re-zero only the buckets you touched, or use a map. Flushing output with `endl` after every answer, or unsynchronised C++ streams, can dominate an otherwise linear program. And rebuilding the prefix table inside the query loop turns $O(n+q)$ back into $O(nq)$ (@sec-pref-p2-b, @sec-arr-p5).
:::

**14. You need the *longest* subarray with sum $k$, not the count. What changes in the hash-map walk, and why?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The map stores each prefix value's **first** index instead of its count, and is never overwritten. For a right end $j$, every left end $i$ with $P[i] = P[j]-k$ works, and the longest range uses the smallest such $i$ — the first occurrence. For the *shortest* range you would store the latest index and overwrite. The seed becomes `first[0] = 0`, the index of the empty prefix (@sec-pref-hash).
:::

**15. How does the maximum-subarray problem fit into the prefix-sum picture?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The best subarray ending at $j$ is $P[j] - \min_{i<j} P[i]$, so one pass that keeps the running prefix and the running minimum of earlier prefixes solves it in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space. A prefix *minimum* has no inverse but needs none, because it is anchored at the left end. Kadane's algorithm is the same computation: resetting the running sum when it drops below zero is the moment a new prefix minimum appears (@sec-pref-other).
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **Range sum:** $P[0]=0$, $P[i+1]=P[i]+a[i]$, answer $=P[r]-P[\ell]$. $O(n+q)$.
- **Range add, read once:** $d[\ell]\mathrel{+}=v$, $d[r]\mathrel{-}=v$ with $n+1$ cells, then one prefix pass. $O(n+u)$.
- **Count subarrays by property:** key the running prefix by $p-k$ (equality), $p\!\bmod k$ (divisibility), $p$ itself (balance); seed the empty prefix. $O(n)$.
- **Rectangle sum:** $P[r_2][c_2]-P[r_1][c_2]-P[r_2][c_1]+P[r_1][c_1]$; **rectangle add** uses the mirrored four writes.
- **No inverse?** Build a suffix table and combine: `out[i] = prefix[i] (op) suffix[i]`.
- **Cuts:** $\text{left}=P[k]$, $\text{right}=\text{total}-P[k]$; scan all $k$ unless every element is non-negative.
- **Count in a range:** prefix sums of a 0/1 indicator array. **Modulo $M$:** $(P[r]-P[\ell]+M) \bmod M$.
- **Longest range with sum $k$:** map from prefix value to its *first* index; **best range sum:** $\max_j (P[j] - \min_{i<j} P[i])$.
:::

- A prefix table converts an $O(n)$ question into two array reads; a difference table converts an $O(n)$ update into two writes. They are the same idea seen from opposite ends, and every pattern here is one of those two conversions.
- The convention $P[0]=0$ with half-open ranges is what makes both conversions branch-free — including for the empty range and the whole array.
- Whether an operation admits the range trick is decided by its algebra (associativity plus an inverse), not by how you write the loop. XOR qualifies; min, max and gcd do not, so they get a suffix table instead.
- Counting questions ("how many subarrays sum to $k$") move the work into a hash map or a $k$-bucket array; the seed for the empty prefix is part of the template, not a detail.
- Two dimensions add one more inclusion–exclusion term, and one more chance to get a sign wrong — verify on a rectangle that touches the padded edges.
- Magnitude is part of correctness: prefix tables hold sums of up to $10^5$–$10^6$ inputs, so read the value range with the array size before choosing `int` (@sec-arr-cost).
- Positivity is part of correctness too: it is the difference between a monotone predicate you can search and a scan you must run (@sec-pref-p6).
- What this chapter deliberately does *not* handle: updates and queries interleaved. That is a Fenwick tree or a segment tree, and it is the reason the difference array's "read once at the end" clause exists.

## Practice ladder

Ordered by concept, following the six patterns: each group starts one step beyond a solved problem and adds one idea at a time.

::: {.practice}
- [LC 303 · Range Sum Query - Immutable](https://leetcode.com/problems/range-sum-query-immutable/){difficulty="Easy"} — the table, with the query already handed to you.
- [CF 313B · Ilya and Queries](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/313/B){rating="1100"} — prefix *counts*: turn "adjacent equal characters" into a 0/1 array first.
- [LC 2559 · Count Vowel Strings in Ranges](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-vowel-strings-in-ranges/){difficulty="Medium"} — an indicator array and its prefix table, many range counts.
- [LC 2090 · K Radius Subarray Averages](https://leetcode.com/problems/k-radius-subarray-averages/){difficulty="Medium"} — fixed-length range sums, read from the table.
- [LC 1588 · Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays/){difficulty="Easy"} — enumerate ranges with a table instead of re-summing them.
- [LC 1732 · Find the Highest Altitude](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-the-highest-altitude/){difficulty="Easy"} — a running prefix where the answer is a max over prefixes.
- [CF 279B · Books](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/279/B){rating="1400"} — prefix sums plus a two-pointer; only valid because every value is positive.
- [LC 930 · Binary Subarrays With Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-subarrays-with-sum/){difficulty="Medium"} — count ranges with a given sum in the non-negative regime, where a window also works.
- [CF 873B · Balanced Substring](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/873/B){rating="1500"} — the $\pm1$ transform, then the longest range between equal prefixes.
- [LC 525 · Contiguous Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/contiguous-array/){difficulty="Medium"} — the same transform with a first-index map.
- [LC 523 · Continuous Subarray Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/continuous-subarray-sum/){difficulty="Medium"} — remainder collisions with a *first-seen index* map instead of counts.
- [CF 1344A · Hilbert's Hotel](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1344/A){rating="1600"} — modular collisions, with the negative-remainder trap as the whole puzzle.
- [LC 2845 · Count of Interesting Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-of-interesting-subarrays/){difficulty="Medium"} — a remainder bucket over prefix *counts*, in one pass.
- [CF 1320A · Journey Planning](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1320/A){rating="1400"} — subtract the index from every value, then group equal keys: the Good Subarrays rewrite.
- [CF 1015A · Points in Segments](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1015/A){rating="800"} — mark coverage, read once: the difference array at its smallest.
- [LC 1893 · Check if All the Integers in a Range Are Covered](https://leetcode.com/problems/check-if-all-the-integers-in-a-range-are-covered/){difficulty="Easy"} — coverage with a count instead of a sum.
- [LC 3427 · Sum of Variable Length Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-variable-length-subarrays/){difficulty="Easy"} — how many ranges cover each cell: a coverage count in disguise.
- [CF 816B · Karen and Coffee](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/816/B){rating="1400"} — a difference array for coverage, then a prefix table over the result: both directions in one problem.
- [LC 1094 · Car Pooling](https://leetcode.com/problems/car-pooling/){difficulty="Medium"} — passengers on and off at stops: the event sweep of a difference array.
- [LC 3355 · Zero Array Transformation I](https://leetcode.com/problems/zero-array-transformation-i/){difficulty="Medium"} — decide feasibility from accumulated range adds.
- [CF 276C · Little Girl and Maximum Sum](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/276/C){rating="1500"} — count how often each index is queried, then sort: coverage feeding an optimisation.
- [LC 3356 · Zero Array Transformation II](https://leetcode.com/problems/zero-array-transformation-ii/){difficulty="Medium"} — the same difference array searched over a monotone predicate.
- [LC 995 · Minimum Number of K Consecutive Bit Flips](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-k-consecutive-bit-flips/){difficulty="Hard"} — a difference array over parity, with a forced greedy choice.
- [CSES 1652 · Forest Queries](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1652) — the 2D table over a binary grid, many submatrix sums.
- [LC 1314 · Matrix Block Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/matrix-block-sum/){difficulty="Medium"} — clipped rectangles; the padding saves you four branches.
- [LC 1074 · Number of Submatrices That Sum to Target](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-submatrices-that-sum-to-target/){difficulty="Hard"} — Pattern 2 and Pattern 4 together: fix two rows, then count with a hash map.
- [LC 1442 · Count Triplets That Can Form Two Arrays of Equal XOR](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-triplets-that-can-form-two-arrays-of-equal-xor/){difficulty="Medium"} — equal prefix XORs, counted like equal prefix sums.
- [CF 1847C · Vampiric Powers, anyone?](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1847/C){rating="1400"} — every reachable value is a range XOR, i.e. the XOR of two prefixes.
- [LC 53 · Maximum Subarray](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-subarray/){difficulty="Medium"} — prefix sum against a running prefix minimum.
- [LC 42 · Trapping Rain Water](https://leetcode.com/problems/trapping-rain-water/){difficulty="Hard"} — a prefix-max table against a suffix-max table.
- [CF 1029C · Maximal Intersection](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1029/C){rating="1600"} — "everything except one segment" with prefix and suffix intersections, the except-self shape for max and min.
- [LC 1031 · Maximum Sum of Two Non-Overlapping Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-sum-of-two-non-overlapping-subarrays/){difficulty="Medium"} — a cut, with the best window on each side.
- [CF 466C · Number of Ways](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/466/C){rating="1700"} — three-way split with equal sums, including the all-zero case that breaks naive counting.
- [LC 862 · Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K](https://leetcode.com/problems/shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k/){difficulty="Hard"} — negatives return: prefix sums plus a monotone deque, a preview of later chapters.
:::

## Further reading

- [USACO Guide — Introduction to Prefix Sums](https://usaco.guide/silver/prefix-sums) — the same $P[r]-P[\ell]$ derivation for contest programmers, with graded practice problems.
- [USACO Guide — More Prefix Sums](https://usaco.guide/silver/more-prefix-sums) — 2D prefix sums and counting-by-remainder, i.e. @sec-pref-2d and @sec-pref-hash with contest problems attached.
- [Wikipedia — Prefix sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefix_sum) — the general statement that any associative binary operator gives a prefix structure, which is the algebra behind @sec-pref-other.
- [Wikipedia — Inclusion–exclusion principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclusion%E2%80%93exclusion_principle) — why the 2D query adds the corner back, and where the alternating signs come from (@sec-pref-2d).
- [CP-Algorithms — The Inclusion-Exclusion Principle](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/inclusion-exclusion.html) — the same sign argument written for a competitive-programming audience, with bitmask enumeration of the general case.
- [`itertools.accumulate` — Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html#itertools-accumulate) — the standard-library prefix scan; note the `initial=` parameter, which is exactly the $P[0]=0$ cell.
- [`std::partial_sum` — cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/partial_sum) — the C++ standard prefix scan, including the overload with a custom binary operation (and why it is the wrong tool when you need the padded $n+1$ table).
- [`numpy.cumsum` — NumPy documentation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.cumsum.html) — vectorised prefix sums with an `axis` argument; one call per axis builds the 2D table of @sec-pref-2d (without the zero border).
